opening.headline: As the model's capabilities increase, you learn by what standards the provider controls risk and how to read the safety frameworks of the three providers in the same framework.
body: Models become more complex with each generation. Among them are areas such as biology and chemistry, cyber, and AI research automation, where the damage can be very high if misused or out of control. For organizations adopting a model, it is difficult to plan without knowing what protections will be in place at what capability level.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind have each released safety frameworks to reveal risk areas, thresholds, and responses. In this lesson, we look at the three frameworks one by one and compare them with the same four questions: risk areas and thresholds, response, and disclosure. Next, we explain the impact of access-restricted functions on work plans with examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain risk areas, thresholds, and responses of the Preparedness Framework, Responsible Scaling Policy, and Frontier Safety Framework
Evaluate the impact of the framework on your organization’s model adoption plans

screens.title: By what standards does the provider control when model capacity increases?
screens.lead:
Read the situation below from the perspective of an organization looking to adopt the model. As capabilities increase, it is time to think about why separate control standards are needed.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

Google DeepMind FSF added Tracking Capability Levels (TCLs) to some areas in v3.1 on 2026-04-17. Rather than reading it as a CCL-only framework, distinguish between two levels of purpose and application areas.

paragraphs: Models become more complex with each generation. It has become possible to read and modify code or perform lengthy tasks independently by switching between multiple tools. These abilities can be of great help at work, but if misused, the same abilities can be very damaging.

There are areas in particular where misuse can be very damaging. Representative examples include risks in the biological and chemical fields, cyber attack capabilities, and the ability of AI to automate AI research on its own. In these areas, it may be too late to respond after an incident, so it must be controlled according to pre-determined standards before the capability reaches a certain level.

The concerns of the introductory organization are different. If you don't know what protections are available at what competency level for the model you plan to use, your plans will falter when delivery conditions change. So each of the three providers has published its safety framework, revealing risk areas, thresholds, and responses.
The questions for this class are: What are the common structures and differences between the three frameworks, and how do they affect our organization’s introduction plan?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What information do you need to know during the planning stage to ensure your work does not stop even if model delivery conditions suddenly change? Think again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let's think about whether we have ever seen similar step-by-step control in our daily lives.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question on your own first and then select it, the instructor will organize it for you. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever felt that the terms and conditions of use have changed when a new model is released?
items.answer: When a new model is released, not only the performance but also the delivery method and terms of use may change. Even if the change may seem sudden, looking at the provider's framework can sometimes explain what the criteria is. In this lesson you will learn how to read those standards.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a phased approach to releasing high-risk systems? Like pharmaceutical or construction safety.
items.answer: In areas with high risk, it is common to increase the verification level and safety standards depending on the size of the risk. Drugs go through several stages of verification and the larger the building, the more stringent the standards. The model safety framework follows the same idea of ​​proportional protection, increasing safeguards as capability increases.

items.prompt: Do you know where to check the safety standards for the models we use in our work?
items.answer: Providers publish safety frameworks, policy documents and risk reports. If the adopter knows where these documents are, they can use them as a basis for model selection and approval procedures. Without knowing, it is difficult to gauge the impact of changes to the terms of delivery.

screens.outro: Now, let's first take a look at OpenAI's Preparedness Framework as a structural diagram.

screens.title: OpenAI Preparedness Framework
screens.lead: If you select the number marker in the picture, a description of each element of the Preparedness Framework will appear. Follow the flow from risk selection criteria to decision making.

visual.alt: Preparedness Framework structure diagram with priority response criteria, tracking/research categories, capability thresholds, safeguards, and review in that order.
labels: Five priority response criteria (plausibility, measurability, severity, complete novelty, immediate or irreversible)
Review of safety devices and Safety Advisory Group

markers.label: Priority response criteria
markers.title: 1. Five criteria for deciding what to respond to first
markers.body: The Preparedness Framework is a process for tracking and preparing for capabilities that could cause significant harm. I believe that as capabilities grow, real-world safety measures become more important. Five criteria determine which abilities to track. The risk must be plausible, measurable, serious, novel, and immediate or irreversible.

markers.label: tracking category
markers.title: 2. Tracking Category: Areas where evaluation and safeguards are mature
markers.body: The tracking category is an area where evaluation and safeguards are already mature. There are three abilities: biological and chemical abilities, cybersecurity abilities, and AI self-improvement abilities. This is also a dual-use area with great benefits for science, engineering and research, so investing early in measurements and safeguards is important.

markers.label: Research Category
markers.title: 3. Category of study: Area in which the assessment is being developed.
markers.body: The research category is an area that can cause serious harm but does not yet meet the standards of the tracking category. Long-range autonomy, intentional degradation (sandbagging), autonomous replication and adaptation, fail-safe compromise, and nuclear/radioactivity are current focuses. We are developing threat models and advanced assessments.

markers.label: ability threshold
markers.title: 4. Two levels of ability threshold
markers.body: The threshold is simplified to two steps: High abilities are abilities that can amplify existing paths to significant damage, while Critical abilities are abilities that can open unprecedented new paths. Required actions are specified for each stage.

markers.label: Safeguards and Reviews
markers.title: 5. Safety measures and internal review before distribution
markers.body: Systems that reach High must have safeguards in place to sufficiently reduce risk before deployment. Systems that have reached critical status require safety devices even during development. The Safety Advisory Group, comprised of safety officers from multiple departments, reviews and recommends whether safety measures are sufficient, and the final decision is made by management. Persuasion risks are not addressed in this framework but through separate pathways such as Model Specification and Use Restrictions.

screens.outro: Next, let's see how Anthropic addresses the same problem.

screens.title: Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy
screens.lead: Take a step-by-step look at the elements that make up Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). Select the arrow to advance to the next element.

steps.title: core promise
steps.body: As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

steps.title: Principle. proportional protection
steps.body: The principle is proportional protection. Ensure that safety measures grow in proportion to the potential hazard. This means that heavy controls are not applied to models with low risk, but more stringent controls are applied to models with high risk.

steps.title: Risk assessment and mitigation measures
steps.body: Determine which risks are assessed and responded to, with what evidence. Even if the risk names are similar, categories in past versions do not correspond directly to categories in the current version.

steps.title: Distinction between safety roadmap and promise
steps.body: Distinguish between roadmap goals and policy-required actions. Improvement goals should not be read as an obligation to immediately stop training and distribution.

steps.title: Regular risk reports
steps.body: Anthropic regularly publishes risk reports describing our risk assessment and preparedness status. The report includes some edits, but includes a section explaining the scope and transparency of the edits. This is a device that allows the basis for risk judgment to be confirmed from the outside.

steps.title: Revision and reporting procedures
steps.body: The policy is a document that is repeatedly revised, and the text and redline for each version are released together. Procedures for reporting policy violations and policies prohibiting retaliation against those who report are also disclosed separately. Even if there are changes, you can keep track of where they have changed.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework.

screens.title: Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. See how Google DeepMind handles competency levels and mitigations.

data.text: The Frontier Safety Framework is a collection of protocols that ensure the most advanced models are trustworthy, sufficiently validated, and aligned with human values. It consists of four components. First, it identifies the capability level of frontier models. Second, it applies protocols to detect whether models have reached that capability level throughout their entire lifecycle. Third, it establishes proactive mitigation plans to reduce risks when the capability level is achieved. Fourth, it involves external stakeholders when necessary. The core unit of this framework is Critical Capability Level, i.e., CCL. Recent revisions have included Harmful manipulative abilities within the risk domain and expanded the scope to include scenarios where operators are prevented from instructing, modifying, or halting models, represented by misalignment. When CCL is reached, external review of safety case is conducted prior to external release, and Large-scale internal deployment is also included in the review process. Mitigation measures are applied as part of standard development processes prior to reaching CCL.

terms.tip: The level of ability of a model to increase the risk of serious damage in the absence of mitigation measures. It serves as a warning level established for each risk area.

It is a powerful manipulative ability that can systematically and significantly change people's beliefs and behavior as they interact in high-risk contexts. It was added as a CCL area through revision.
This is a situation where the model behaves contrary to the operator's intentions. This covers scenarios that impede the operator's ability to direct, modify, or stop the model.
A detailed analysis showing that the risk has been reduced to a manageable level. When CCL is reached, this review is done prior to external release.

This is a case where it is widely used within the organization rather than released externally. In particular, internal distribution can be a risk in machine learning research and development capabilities, so it is subject to review.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the three frameworks one by one, let's compare them in one table.

screens.title: Table of risk areas of the three-company framework
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to compare the terms in which the three providers express their risk areas and levels of response. Although the terminology is different, the structure is similar.

data.caption: Comparing the safety frameworks of three providers
columns: Terms that define the level of response
rows: Biology/Chemistry, Cybersecurity, AI Self-Improvement (tracking categories). Long-distance autonomy, etc. (research category)
According to the evaluation maturity, it is divided into tracking category and research category. Persuasion risks are covered in a separate path, such as in the Model Spec.
Chemical and biological hazards, automated research and development, high-risk misalignment, etc.
Follows the principle of proportional protection. We disclose regular risk reports and revision history by version.
Accelerated machine learning research and development, harmful manipulation, misalignment, etc.
Once the CCL is reached, a safety case review is conducted prior to external release. Manipulation and misalignment are treated as areas within the framework.
data.notes: Common areas include biological and chemical risks, cyber risks, and risks related to AI research and development automation and autonomy. A common structure is the flow of identifying capabilities, detecting arrival with assessments, applying safeguards when thresholds are reached, and review and release. The differences are the terminology, number of steps, and whether persuasion and manipulation risks are addressed within the framework. For example, Google DeepMind puts harmful manipulation in the realm of CCL, but OpenAI addresses persuasion risks with Model Specifications and usage restrictions outside the framework. The risk areas in the table are examples for each document, so the full list should be checked in the original document. Any parts of the table that appear empty may mean that the provider has categorized the item differently.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the common structure, let us explain through examples how it affects business planning.

screens.title: Commentary: Impact of restricted access functions on business planning
screens.lead: The instructor explains step-by-step the case of an organization that wants to create a security analysis tool. Select the arrows to follow the path the framework takes to influence your plan.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: An organization is planning to create a security analysis tool. The model we want to use in our tool is one whose capabilities in the cyber domain are close to critical mass. The model's ability to find vulnerabilities in code is dual-purpose, allowing it to be used both defensively and offensively.

steps.title: Step 1. What the Framework Requires
steps.body: The framework requires safeguards to sufficiently reduce risk before deployment for capabilities that reach critical mass. The provider provides the model after confirming that this safety device is in place. Safeguards may include operational measures such as access control, monitoring, and use restrictions, as well as training of the model itself.

steps.title: Step 2. Consequences on business
steps.body: As a result, the terms of provision of the function may change or the scope of use may be limited. For example, a particular feature may be available only to some customers or may require additional verification before it is available. It is dangerous for an organization's plans to rely on the assumption that all features of the model will always be available. Especially in projects with tight schedules, the damage is greater when this assumption is broken.

steps.title: Step 3. Compare during the planning stage
steps.body: During the planning phase, we first check whether our business functions overlap with the risk areas disclosed by the provider. If there are overlapping areas, check the documentation to see what action is taken at what threshold. If they don't overlap, record that fact too so you can compare them later when your work expands.

steps.title: Step 4. design an alternative
steps.body: Divide the functional scope to separate parts that may be subject to limitations and those that do not. If a restriction occurs, plan a route to an alternative flow in advance. For example, you can configure human analysts to handle only analysis steps that are close to risk areas. This way, if you run into a limitation, you can replace just that step without having to rebuild the entire tool.

screens.outro: This time, we will summarize the order in which the framework is reflected in the introduction plan.

screens.title: Commentary: Order of incorporating the framework into the introduction plan
screens.lead: The instructor explains the order in which the framework should be checked when planning model introduction. Follow the five steps using the arrows.

steps.title: 1. Identify the risk areas that your work touches.
steps.body: We first determine whether our work touches the risk areas covered by the framework, such as biological/chemical, cyber, and autonomy. This does not apply to most general tasks, but security, research, and automation tasks require confirmation. Also write down the basis for determining that it is not applicable in one line.

steps.title: 2. Read thresholds and responses
steps.body: Read the thresholds and responses for these areas from the provider's framework and risk report. The framework provides structure, and the risk report provides current risk assessment and preparedness. You should read them together to understand both the rules and the current status.

steps.title: 3. Reflect changes when the model changes
steps.body: Plan for changes in the model that may result in different evaluation results and safeguard levels. Include steps to double-check the terms and conditions in your timeline for moving to a new model. If you replace it immediately after hearing that the model has improved, the features that were previously possible may change. Before replacing, ask the same four questions again on the new model's documentation.

steps.title: 4. Add confirmation items to the approval process
steps.body: Include verification of provider-disclosed documentation in your internal approval process. Keeping records of who checked which documents and when makes accountability clear. It is best to keep the check items simple: risk areas, thresholds, required safeguards, and published reports.

steps.title: 5. Have a business continuity plan
steps.body: Have a plan in place to continue work when restrictions arise. Decide in advance the options of replacing it with another model, having a person take over the function, or reducing the scope of use. Finding options after restrictions are in place will result in extended downtime.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will summarize how to read the three documents with the same eyes.

screens.title: Commentary: Eyes to read the framework, risk/threshold/response/disclosure
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate four questions to ask in the same order as you read the framework. When you select a card, it flips over and you can move to the next card with the right arrow.

cards.back: This framework asks what harms are assumed? The areas are different, such as biological/chemical, cyber, autonomy, and manipulation. The same area may have different names and scopes from one provider to another, so our first question is to collate the list of areas.
Ask about the conditions for changing the response. We read OpenAI's High·Critical, Google DeepMind's CCL, and Anthropic's current policy conditions separately.

Ask what safeguards and reviews are in place before deployment or during development. OpenAI reviews the Safety Advisory Group, and Google DeepMind reviews the safety case. How long it takes to respond will affect your adoption schedule.

I am asking whether it is possible to check the report and revision history externally. Anthropic publishes risk reports and version-specific change notes. Broader disclosure allows the adopting organization to proactively read changes in delivery terms. Items that are insufficiently disclosed will be left as questions to be checked directly with the provider.

cards.front: All three documents in the same order
cards.back: Placing the four questions on the three documents in the same order makes comparison easier. Even if the document structure is different, as you fill in the fields for risk, threshold, response, and disclosure, the blank spaces will soon become things to check. This method can also be used when reading a document from a new provider for the first time.

screens.outro: Now let's organize the entire class. The four questions are a tool you can use over and over again every time you read a new document.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: We summarize the common structure of the three frameworks and their impact on adoption plans.

paragraphs: The three frameworks are compared on the same questions: risk identification, assessment, mitigation, judgment and disclosure. OpenAI's High·Critical, Google DeepMind's CCL, and Anthropic RSP's Action·Roadmap·Report are not the same step table.

Risk reports and revision history are external means of checking response status. Unlike general usage policies, the framework addresses controls based on model capabilities rather than scope of prohibited usage. When a critical mass is reached, the model is not stopped but requires safeguards and reviews before deployment.

The organization compares functions that may be subject to limitations with risk areas during the planning stage and prepares alternative paths in advance if limitations arise. The answer to the initial question, what do you need to know to ensure your work does not stop when delivery conditions change, is four things: risk areas, thresholds, response, and disclosure.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Consider which of the capabilities of the model your organization is planning to use that is closest to the risk area, and what alternatives are available if those capabilities are limited.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: In the OpenAI Preparedness Framework, what would you call the threshold for the ability to significantly amplify existing known paths to damage and the ability to open unprecedented new paths?
checks.explain: High is an amplification of an existing path, Critical is an unprecedented new path. High requires safety measures before distribution, and Critical requires safety measures even during development.

wrong.2: Category distinctions are about assessment maturity and not thresholds.
wrong.3: CCL is a term for Google DeepMind, and ASL is a term for Anthropic.

checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The order is High, Critical.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

checks.intro: Organize the content by matching providers with key terms. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Try to connect your provider with the policy elements discussed in this lesson.
right: High and Critical thresholds, tracking and research categories
checks.explain: Each policy has different terms and levels of obligations. Distinguish between what is a requirement and what is a goal in the current version.

checks.intro: Try to remember the order in which you read the framework. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: As you read the framework, try putting the four questions in the same order.
items: Threshold: At what ability level does response vary?
Response: What safeguards are in place before deployment and during development?
Disclosure: Can it be confirmed through the report and revision history?
checks.explain: Comparison becomes easier if you ask the same questions to the three documents in the following order: risk, threshold, response, and disclosure.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. I placed the order correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Imagine a flow that starts with assumed harm and ends with disclosure.

glossary.def: This is the process by which OpenAI tracks and prepares for the ability to cause significant harm.
Governance policy to manage risk in accordance with Anthropic's principles of proportional protection.
A protocol through which Google DeepMind identifies capability levels, detects arrival, and creates mitigation plans.
It is a competency standard that requires stronger safety measures once it reaches that level. There are High, Critical, CCL, etc.
This is a document released by the provider explaining its risk assessment and preparedness status.

misconceptions.myth: A safety framework is a document like a usage policy.
misconceptions.fact: The usage policy determines what users should not do, and the framework sets control standards as model capabilities increase. The subjects covered are different.

misconceptions.myth: When a threshold is reached, the model stops.
misconceptions.fact: When a critical value is reached, safety measures and reviews are required to sufficiently reduce risk before deployment or during development. The model does not automatically break.

misconceptions.myth: The three companies use the same standards and terminology.
misconceptions.fact: The risk areas and structures overlap, but the terminology and phase organization are different. To compare accurately, you need to ask the same questions.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The framework is the governing standard for increasing model capabilities.
All three have a framework of risk areas, thresholds, response, and disclosure.
You can check the status of your response with risk reports and revision documents.
Work planning requires identification of risk areas and alternative routes.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of the model capabilities my organization is considering is closest to the risk area?
